I have owned a few small businesses. One was a bit profitable (enough to pay employees, my bills, invest back into the business, and save some extra cash on the side). One barely broke even. The current one does great, in fact it's doing so well I don't even need to be in the day to day running of it. I get a check in the mail every month and can pursue other interest (not tens of thousands a month, but enough to pay the bills).

Nothing infuriates me more than the media and feel good blogs tricking young entrepreneurs with BULLSHIT stories about how companies that are now worth billions created them from nothing. Obviously, you can be pedantic and say day one they had nothing, but the implication I have seen since I can remember is that you can build a multi billion dollar business with no money and just a passion. The reality is, this isn't how it works save for the extremely, extremely, extremely rare business. Less than 10% of small businesses will survive past 5 years. An estimated half of those that do survive can't even pay their bills and for sure aren't putting excess money into the owners pocket (retirement). Y combinator (one of the largest business start up incubators ever) has a success rate less than 7%. I will happily answer any questions you may have about starting a business (that I can). And below are some bullshit stories you may have heard.

"Google was grown out of a garage!!!!" In reality, they had already received MILLIONS in investments and moved into that garage to help a friend pay their mortgage with investors money.

"Amazon was started out of his garage!!!" Yes, after he left a lucrative career and also got HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS of $ from his parents.

"Steve Jobs created Apple from nothing!" First, they just used homebrew shit and made a shitty computer. They got a local computer seller to give them a PO (purchase order) if they could deliver 50. Then, they got VERY LUCK (a different time my friends) to get all the parts they needed to build them on credit with NO collateral other than the word of the computer shop owner. This would almost NEVER happen today. My first business had to buy EVERYTHING on the spot. You could buy things on credit if you have collateral in todays age (a home, a ton of equipment etc). They also delivered a shit product, they gave the guy fucking circuit boards, not computers. But since he was a man of his word, he paid them. This would almost never happen today. BUT the real growth was the Apple 2. This was what built apple. The Apple one is a foot note. The ONLY reason they got the loan, is because a wealthy man co-signed a $250k loan for them, which is $1.1 MILLION in todays money. How many of you have connections that will sign a loan like that for you?

"Microsoft was started by a college drop out!!!" Yes, a college drop out from a family that could afford to send their kids to private school and then Harvard. The money for the start up was from the two owners wealthy families. Most people won't have that type of advantage in life.

"FUBU was just Daymond selling shirts at small shows!!!" He mortgaged his home for $100k and a chance meeting with LL Cool J put the brand in a music video during his prime.

If you look into the REAL history of many of these "started from nothing" companies you will see the illusion is bullshit. SURE they started with $500 or $1k on day one. But they also immediately received millions or tens of millions in investment. These people were also usually already deep in the industry (either as a job or as a hobby) before they started their businesses.

You might think I am being salty. Or you may be wondering "so what?" Well the point to this post is that if you want to start a business, it's NEVER as easy as "I'll just take this $200 and this idea and I'll make millions!" I see many young businesses owners that think hard work will make all the difference. IT WON'T. Now don't get me wrong you need hard work. You will fail without it. But you won't succeed just because you have it. YOU NEED CAPITAL. You need money to scale. You need money to pay the bills. I am not taking away anything from the people who build these businesses. They made the right moves at the right time, and got in front of the right people. ALL of that is business, and that is what I want to get across. You NEED to be in the right place, at the right time (amazon was a perfect example of this), and have the right connections. You ALSO need to hustle (Daymond is a great example).

Businesses make it from having MONEY. Owning the building is better than renting it (usually). Owning the machine is better than leasing it. Having the inventory on the shelf is important. Are you looking to start a business? Cool, just remember, you WILL need to get capital at some point. I would say a handful of people in history have ever made it without funding. So as you read these things for inspiration, make sure to think like a business owner. HOW did they get that first order funded? HOW did they pay their bills before the first sale? HOW did they go from the garage to 50 employees in a few month?
Don't fall for the media telling you that companies like Google, Amazon, and Microsoft came from nothing. A quick entrprenurial PSA.

Great write up. You have some very salient points here. I would add that the time in which some of these businesses started also played a huge role in their success. These businesses were early in their fields and the barriers to entry were low. Little or no regulations, no established oversight groups and few or no competitors all helped them tremendously. The Steves at Apple didn't need to comply with RoHS, FCC, UL or any other electronics regulatory stuff to get started. They made their first computers without any regulations to get in their way. Microsoft didn't need to deal with licensing and patents or even copyrights. They simply copied (in design/coding) CP/M and BASIC and made money. The laws were less restrictive and you didn't need much to start a business then.

My most recent attempt to get a business off the ground was a bootstrapping effort. I financed it completely and was doing alright. What killed it for me was the fact that every city, state and federal agency had something I had to comply with or pay in order to just be in business. I didn't have the time to fully comply and run the business. It's not like the early part of the 20th century when someone with $100 could open a food stand or repair shop and do well so long as you treated the customer well. Today you need licenses, inspection, certification, property assessment, equipment certification, code compliance and proper zoning. Miss dotting any 'i' or crossing any 't' and you're out of business. Only the already established players can succeed these days in this sea of regulation. It's by design, of course, because competition and innovation is what they want to avoid. I really do hope Trump does what he promises and reduces the regulations and barriers for small business and not just big corporations.
